questions.sec: Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
questions.q: After fixed plaque rupture, which thrombus–clinical-syndrome pairing is correct in the source's older ACS flowchart?
opts: Platelet-rich incomplete occlusion → chronic stable angina
Critical fibrin-rich occlusion → unstable angina with normal enzymes
questions.exp: The obsolete scheme maps critical fibrin-rich thrombus to STEMI/STE-ACS and incomplete platelet-rich thrombus to NSTE-ACS; normal enzymes mean unstable angina and raised enzymes NSTEMI. (Book p430)

questions.sec: Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
questions.q: What is the current universal definition of acute MI stated on the page?
opts: ST elevation in a single ECG lead
A fixed plaque found on angiography
Myocardial injury plus or minus clinical evidence of myocardial ischaemia
Any chest pain with a positive stress test
questions.exp: The page replaces the older model with myocardial injury ± clinical evidence of myocardial ischaemia. (Book p430)

questions.sec: Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
questions.q: Which troponin pattern fulfils the page's definition of myocardial injury?
opts: A stable value below the 50th percentile
One high troponin with no serial measurement
At least one value above the 99th percentile with an acute rise and fall
questions.exp: Myocardial injury is cardiac troponin T/I with at least one value above the 99th percentile and an acute rise and fall. (Book p430)

questions.sec: Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
questions.q: A septic ICU patient has elevated troponin without evidence of acute coronary ischaemia. Which category of cause is the page illustrating?
questions.exp: Non-cardiac causes listed include sepsis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, CKD, critical illness and pulmonary embolism. Cardiac causes include myocarditis, Takotsubo, defibrillator shocks, tachyarrhythmia and spasm/embolism/dissection. (Book p430)

questions.sec: Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
questions.q: A patient with sustained tachyarrhythmia develops myocardial oxygen demand excess and troponin elevation. Which mechanism category is explicitly shown?
questions.exp: The causes tree lists increased O2 demand from tachyarrhythmia and decreased supply from spasm, embolism or dissection. (Book p430)

questions.sec: Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
questions.q: Which clinical finding is one of the page's five forms of evidence for myocardial ischaemia?
questions.exp: Clinical evidence listed: symptoms, new ECG changes, pathological Q waves, imaging evidence of new RWMA, and angiographic evidence of coronary thrombus. (Book p431)

questions.sec: Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
questions.q: Which MI subtype is defined by demand–supply mismatch, with ICU patients and severe anaemia given as examples?
questions.exp: Type 1 is atherothrombotic occlusion; Type 2 is supply/demand mismatch (ICU patients, severe anaemia); Type 3 sudden cardiac death; Type 4 post-PCI; Type 5 post-CABG. (Book p431)

questions.sec: Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
questions.q: Which universal MI subtype is related to percutaneous coronary intervention?
questions.exp: The list gives Type 4 as post-percutaneous coronary intervention and Type 5 as post-coronary artery bypass graft. (Book p431)

questions.sec: Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
questions.q: Ultra-sensitive troponin assays can detect enzyme elevation down to approximately which concentration in the source?
questions.exp: The graph note says ultrasensitive troponin assays can detect as low as 0.01 ng/mL of enzyme elevation. (Book p431)

questions.sec: Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
questions.q: A rising/falling troponin above the 99th-percentile URL occurs with acute ischaemia and plaque rupture/erosion. What diagnosis does the source flowchart assign?
questions.exp: Rise/fall with acute ischaemia is acute MI; the atherosclerosis/thrombosis arm is Type 1 (plaque rupture/erosion). Without acute ischaemia it is acute injury; stable troponin is chronic injury. (Book p431)

questions.sec: Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
questions.q: A stable troponin elevation in a patient with structural heart disease or chronic kidney disease is classified as:
questions.exp: The stable-troponin branch is chronic myocardial injury and gives structural heart disease and CKD as examples. (Book p431)

questions.q: How does the page distinguish reinfarction from recurrence by timing?
opts: Reinfarction within 28 days; recurrence after 28 days
Reinfarction after 90 days; recurrence within 90 days
Reinfarction within 24 hours; recurrence after one week
questions.exp: The table defines reinfarction within 28 days and recurrence after 28 days. (Book p432)

questions.q: For suspected reinfarction/recurrence, what serial troponin change is requested by the source?
opts: More than 20% increase between immediate and 3–6-hour values
A fall of more than 50% over 7 days
questions.exp: Two troponin values are obtained immediately and 3–6 h later; a >20% increase is specified. The table says no role for CPK-MB. (Book p432)

questions.q: Which culprit-lesion process is most common and more associated with men and elevated cholesterol?
questions.exp: Plaque rupture is 60–70% (most common), associated with men and elevated cholesterol; erosion 30–40% is associated with younger females and smoking. (Book p432)

questions.q: Which feature is part of the page's vulnerable-plaque profile?
opts: Thick fibrous cap with abundant smooth muscle
questions.exp: Vulnerable plaque features: thin cap, necrotic lipid core >40%, increased macrophages, reduced smooth-muscle cell content and spotty calcification. (Book p432)

questions.q: A chronically underperfused myocardium has reduced function but viable tissue on evaluation. Which term is correct?
questions.exp: Hibernating myocardium is chronic, viable and has reduced function due to low perfusion; MRI should be used for evaluation. (Book p432)

questions.q: After relief of acute ischaemia, perfusion is restored but function remains reduced for several hours in viable tissue. Which term applies?
questions.exp: Stunned myocardium is acute/post-ischaemic: restoring perfusion for a few hours precedes low function in viable tissue. (Book p432)

questions.q: A patient has rest angina lasting more than 20 minutes, new severe crescendo symptoms, ST depression/T inversion and elevated troponin. What diagnosis is most consistent?
questions.exp: NSTEMI features listed are rest angina >20 min, new-onset severe/crescendo angina, ST depression/T inversion and elevated troponin. (Book p433)

questions.q: Which score determines mortality risk in NSTEMI according to this page?
questions.exp: The NSTEMI feature list states TIMI score determines mortality risk. (Book p433)

questions.q: An Indian patient in the source's typical NSTEMI age range presents with atypical symptoms; what sex pattern is stated for India?
questions.exp: Clinical presentation states age 40–50 in India (50–60 outside), females > males in India (reverse outside), vague symptoms in females and absent classic pain in diabetic patients. (Book p433)

questions.q: Significant ST depression in the page's examples is associated with which acute coronary syndrome?
questions.exp: The lower ECG caption identifies significant ST depression as NSTEMI; the comparison example is non-significant ST depression. (Book p433)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: Which chest-pain descriptor has the highest positive likelihood ratio for AMI in the source table?
opts: Radiation to the right arm or shoulder
questions.exp: The table gives right arm/shoulder radiation 4.7 (0.9–12.0), both arms 4.1, exertion 2.4, left arm 2.3, diaphoresis 2.0, nausea/vomiting 1.9 and pressure 1.3. (Book p434)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: A middle-aged patient is woken by new chest pain and cannot return to sleep. How does the source frame this presentation?
questions.exp: ACA note: new chest pain in middle-aged/elderly, night presentation or being forced awake and unable to sleep is ‘cardiac unless proved otherwise.’ (Book p434)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: Which symptom is included as an angina equivalent?
questions.exp: Angina equivalents listed are dyspnoea, fatigue, diaphoresis and atypical-site pain. (Book p434)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: The page gives which one-month mortality rate for care after reperfusion?
questions.exp: Management continuum: pre-CCU morphine/sedation 30% one-month mortality; CCU beta-blocker/defibrillator 15%; reperfusion with thrombolysis/PCI 5%. (Book p434)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: Which two measures are listed under the source's reperfusion arm?
questions.exp: The source places thrombolysis and percutaneous intervention under reperfusion (since 1975). (Book p434)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: What is the most common immediate lesion in STEMI/STE-ACS according to the page?
opts: Acute total occlusion due to plaque rupture
questions.exp: STEMI salient feature: acute total occlusion due to plaque rupture (most common). (Book p435)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: Which artery is listed as most commonly involved in STEMI?
questions.exp: The artery list ranks LAD most common, then RCA, then LCx. (Book p435)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: What time window is called the ‘golden hours’ for progression of myocardial damage?
questions.exp: Golden hours are the first 6 h. After 6 h from pain onset, only one-sixth of myocardium remains viable in the source. (Book p435)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: Reperfusion is performed after 6 hours of chest pain. Which source-stated benefit remains the emphasis?
opts: Reduce pain and prevent electrical/mechanical complications
questions.exp: Before 6 h myocardium can be salvaged; after 6 h the stated aims are pain reduction and prevention of electrical/mechanical complications. (Book p435)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: The central primary goal of PCI/lysis is expressed how on the mortality-salvage graph?
questions.exp: The graph says opening the artery is the primary goal (PCI/lysis) and time to treatment is critical for mortality/salvage. (Book p435)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: Which is listed as a determinant of salvageable myocardium?
questions.exp: Determinants listed are collaterals, myocardial oxygen demand and ischaemic preconditioning. (Book p436)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: What principle is emphasised above the STEMI target-time flowchart?
opts: ECG may be deferred until after transfer
Reopening the artery matters more than the mode of reperfusion
Thrombolysis is always superior to PCI
questions.exp: The source specifically notes reopening the artery is more important than the mode of reperfusion. (Book p436)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: From chest pain to first medical contact, what target is printed?
questions.exp: The flowchart sets first medical contact <10 min and defines it as medical/paramedical staff able to take/interpret ECG and use a defibrillator. (Book p436)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: A 24-hour PCI centre is available and diagnosis-to-wire-crossing time can be below 60 minutes. What route does the source direct?
opts: Wire crossing within 90 minutes (with 30 minutes allowed for transfer)
questions.exp: If a 24-hour PCI centre is available and diagnosis-to-wire crossing <60 min, wire crossing is to be done within 90 min (+30 min transfer). (Book p436)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: A patient cannot be shifted to a PCI centre within 120 minutes. What reperfusion option and time are specified?
opts: Thrombolysis within 10 minutes with tenecteplase or reteplase
questions.exp: If timely transfer is not possible, thrombolysis within 10 min with tenecteplase or reteplase is shown, then transfer to a PCI centre. (Book p436)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: After lysis, ST resolution at 60–90 minutes is below 70%. Which next step is listed?
opts: No further intervention because lysis is successful
questions.exp: ST resolution >70% is successful and leads to pharmaco-invasive PCI; <70% is unsuccessful and calls for rescue/emergency PCI. (Book p436)

questions.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
questions.q: Following successful thrombolysis, the pharmaco-invasive approach schedules PCI within:
questions.exp: Successful lysis is followed by PCI within 2–24 hours to prevent recurrence of thrombus formation. (Book p436)

questions.q: Which thrombolytic is non-fibrin-specific, antigenic, and has the lowest source-listed risk of intracranial haemorrhage?
questions.exp: Streptokinase is non-specific, 50% potent, antigenic, has lowest ICH risk and is 1.5 million U in 100 mL NS over 1 hour. (Book p437)

questions.q: Which thrombolytic is described as having maximal fibrin specificity and highest fibrin selectivity?
questions.exp: Tenecteplase is specific (max), 75% potent, half-life 10–12 min, dose 0.5 mg/kg, and highest fibrin selectivity. (Book p437)

questions.q: What reteplase regimen is printed in the agent table?
opts: 10 U in two doses 30 minutes apart
questions.exp: Reteplase is specific, 80% potent and dosed 10 U ×2, 30 min apart. (Book p437)

questions.q: What characteristic distinguishes alteplase in the table?
questions.exp: Alteplase is specific, 75% potent and has a very short 4–8 minute half-life. (Book p437)

questions.q: Within the first hour of ACS, how does the source compare thrombolysis with PCI for effect?
questions.exp: The source states effect within 1 h of ACS: thrombolysis = PCI, while PCI is otherwise more superior and mandatory after thrombolysis. (Book p437)

questions.q: What is the source’s timing comparison for thrombolysis?
opts: Benefits exceed risk within 6–12 h; risk exceeds benefits after 12 h
Only the first 15 minutes are useful
questions.exp: Thrombolysis benefits > risk within 6–12 h, risk > benefit after 12 h; pre-hospital lysis is noted to have a great outcome. (Book p437)

questions.q: Which initial aspirin dose and formulation are listed for thrombolysis?
questions.exp: Loading-dose section gives aspirin 325 mg, non-enteric chewable; statins: atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg. (Book p437)

questions.q: An IWMI patient is bradycardic after a proximal RCA lesion and shows V1–V2 discordance. Which associated diagnosis is noted?
questions.exp: Note: RVMI has hypotension, clear lung and raised JVP; IWMI has bradycardia due to proximal occlusion and V1–V2 discordance. (Book p437)

questions.q: What clopidogrel loading dose is stated for an adult undergoing thrombolysis?
questions.exp: For thrombolysis: clopidogrel 300 mg adult dose; age >75 receives 75 mg, with blood-cholesterol monitoring at 3–6 months. (Book p438)

questions.q: For PCI, which P2Y12 loading strategy is marked ‘best’ on the page?
questions.exp: PCI section: aspirin/statin same dose; ticagrelor 180 mg best, clopidogrel 600 mg, prasugrel 60 mg. (Book p438)

questions.q: What two flow goals define the stated aim of PCI?
opts: No ST change and zero troponin
TIMI 3 epicardial flow and MPG 3 microvascular flow
TIMI 1 and MPG 1 to prevent bleeding
Normal venous flow and lymphatic drainage
questions.exp: PCI aim is restore normal epicardial coronary flow (TIMI 3) and attain normal microvascular flow (MPG 3). (Book p438)

questions.q: After thrombolysis a patient develops hypotension and bradycardia. What does the source interpret this combination as?
questions.exp: Post-lysis hypotension + bradycardia indicates vessels reopening; hypertension + tachycardia suggests noncompliance/allergic reaction. (Book p438)

questions.q: Post-lysis blood pressure is low and prognosis is poor. Which cause–action pairing is correct?
opts: Cardiogenic shock → assess IVC diameter only
questions.exp: Low BP causes listed: hypovolaemia → assess IVC; RVMI (IWMI) → IV fluids; cardiogenic shock → intra-aortic balloon pump. (Book p438)

questions.q: Why are anticoagulants continued after thrombolysis according to the flowchart?
opts: Raw plaque areas are exposed and recurrence must be prevented
questions.exp: Prevention of recurrence: post-thrombolysis raw areas exposed → anticoagulants. LMWH: enoxaparin 30 mg bolus plus 1 mg/kg SC BD until revascularisation/8 days; UFH also listed. (Book p438)

questions.q: Within what timeframe does the note say young thrombus responds better to lysis?
questions.exp: Young thrombus responds better if lysed within 1–2 h; if primary PCI cannot be performed after STEMI diagnosis, fibrinolytic therapy is recommended within 12 h. (Book p438)

questions.q: Which agents are the GP IIb–IIIa inhibitors listed for downstream bailout therapy?
questions.exp: GP IIb–IIIa inhibitors are abciximab, tirofiban, eptifibatide; use is downstream bailout in cath lab if no TIMI 3/MPG 3 flow or high thrombus burden. (Book p439)

questions.q: When initiated within the first 24 hours, which two drug classes are stated to confer survival advantage?
questions.exp: ACE inhibitors/beta-blockers have survival advantage if started within first 24 h, but are avoided with heart-failure signs/low-output state. (Book p439)

questions.q: A PCI centre is available for a STEMI patient. Which initial regimen matches the source algorithm?
opts: Aspirin 325 mg, ticagrelor 180 mg or clopidogrel 600 mg, and rosuvastatin 40 mg
Clopidogrel 75 mg alone and delayed statin
Tenecteplase 0.5 mg/kg before angiography in all cases
questions.exp: Available PCI centre branch lists aspirin 325 mg, ticagrelor 180 mg or clopidogrel 600 mg, rosuvastatin 40 mg, then cath lab. (Book p439)

questions.q: No PCI centre is available. Which thrombolysis branch is printed?
opts: Clopidogrel 300 mg plus tenecteplase 0.5 mg/kg, then repeat ECG in 60–90 min
questions.exp: No-centre branch: thrombolysis with clopidogrel 300 mg + tenecteplase 0.5 mg/kg, repeat ECG after 60–90 min, then enoxaparin 30 mg IV and pharmaco-invasive/rescue PCI. (Book p439)

questions.q: After normal TIMI 3 and MPG 3 flow, which long-term schedule is shown?
opts: Rosuvastatin 20 mg and aspirin 75 mg lifelong; clopidogrel 75 mg for one year
questions.exp: CCU/discharge box: rosuvastatin 20 mg lifelong, aspirin 75 mg lifelong, clopidogrel 75 mg ×1 year. (Book p439)

questions.q: Which item is NOT listed as a contraindication to thrombolysis on the page?
opts: Intracranial haemorrhage or structural cerebrovascular mass
Stroke within three months (except acute stroke within 4.5 h)
Uncomplicated remote appendicectomy ten years ago
questions.exp: Contraindications include intracranial haemorrhage/structural mass, recent stroke, bleeding disorder/aortic dissection, recent severe head/facial trauma, intracranial/intraspinal surgery, uncontrolled HTN, and recent streptokinase use. (Book p439)

questions.q: An RVMI patient is hypotensive with elevated JVP and clear lungs. Which hemodynamic treatment appears on the STEMI-complication page?
questions.exp: Hemodynamic complication: RVMI hypotension presents with raised JVP and clear lungs; management is IV fluids. (Book p440)

questions.q: How much myocardial damage is associated with acute LV failure in the source complication chart?
questions.exp: Acute LVF is linked to 25% myocardial damage and proximal LAD lesion; cardiogenic shock to 40% damage/proximal LAD. (Book p440)

questions.q: Which lesion–electrical-complication pair is correct?
opts: Proximal LAD lesion → isolated atrial flutter
questions.exp: Electrical complications: RCA lesion → atrial arrhythmias; proximal LAD lesion → VT/VF. (Book p440)

questions.q: Three to five days after MI, a patient develops pain and a new murmur at the left lower sternal border with a thrill. Which mechanical complication is described?
questions.exp: Septal rupture is described as rare, after 3–5 days, with pain, new LLSB murmur and thrill. (Book p440)

questions.q: Sudden pulseless electrical activity with no BP/pulse and tamponade after infarction is most suggestive of:
questions.exp: Free-wall rupture causes electromechanical dissociation/PEA, no BP/no pulse and tamponade, with poor prognosis. (Book p440)

questions.q: Acute pulmonary oedema after an RCA infarct is attributed to involvement of which structure?
opts: Posteromedial papillary muscle causing acute MR
questions.exp: Acute MR: RCA involvement affects posteromedial papillary muscle and presents as acute pulmonary oedema. (Book p440)

questions.q: Why does the page state thrombolytics have no role in NSTEMI?
opts: All NSTEMI cases have normal ECGs
The thrombus is platelet-rich with reduced fibrin content
questions.exp: NSTEMI pathogenesis is plaque rupture in elderly/comorbid people with critical/subtotal occlusion, ST/T changes, platelet-rich thrombus and decreased fibrin, so no thrombolytic role. (Book p440)

questions.q: Chest pain has increased in nature, duration beyond 20 minutes and frequency and is not relieved by nitrates or rest. Which presentation is being described?
questions.exp: Clinical presentation on p441 describes increasing nature/duration (>20 min)/frequency and pain not relieved by nitrates/rest. (Book p441)

questions.q: Which initial treatment bundle is listed for NSTE-ACS on this page?
opts: Oxygen if SpO2 <90%, aspirin 325 mg, rosuvastatin 40 mg, SL nitrate and morphine
questions.exp: Treatment: O2 if SpO2<90%, aspirin 325 mg chewable non-enteric, rosuvastatin 40 mg, SL nitrate 5 mg repeated three times, morphine, PCI within 24 h (high risk within 2 h). (Book p441)

questions.q: What is the source’s treatment of choice in its NSTE-ACS ‘landmark changes’ note?
questions.exp: Landmark changes list intervention-based guideline: PCI TOC; angiography within 24 h (high risk 2 h), with P2Y12 inhibitor in cath lab. (Book p441)

questions.q: Which peri-interventional enoxaparin dose is written for NSTE-ACS before reaching the cath lab?
questions.exp: Peri-interventional anticoagulation: enoxaparin 0.5 mg/kg bolus until cath lab. (Book p441)

questions.q: Which P2Y12 loading dose is given for prasugrel in the NSTE-ACS cath-lab list?
questions.exp: Cath-lab loading options: prasugrel 60 mg, ticagrelor 180 mg, or clopidogrel 600 mg. (Book p441)

questions.q: After discharge, which source schedule is stated for dual antiplatelet therapy?
opts: Ticagrelor 90 mg BD for one year, or clopidogrel 75 mg OD for one year, or prasugrel 10 mg for one year
questions.exp: After discharge: aspirin 75 mg lifelong, rosuvastatin 20 mg lifelong, and ticagrelor 90 mg BD ×1 y or clopidogrel 75 mg OD ×1 y or prasugrel 10 mg ×1 y (best). (Book p441)

units.title: 1. Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
units.sec: Universal MI Definition, Injury & MI Types
units.guide:
The obsolete plaque-only model is contrasted with the current injury-plus-ischaemia definition.
Troponin kinetics and non-ischaemic causes are separated from acute MI.
Universal MI subtypes follow immediately after the diagnostic framework.

units.title: 2. Reinfarction, Vulnerable Plaque & NSTEMI Recognition
units.guide:
Timing differentiates reinfarction from recurrence.
Culprit pathology and plaque morphology are then ordered before NSTEMI features.
Source-specific prevalence and demographic statements are preserved.

units.title: 3. Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
units.sec: Acute Chest Pain, STEMI Salvage & Reperfusion Timing
units.guide:
Likelihood features of chest pain precede the treatment-mortality timeline.
STEMI pathophysiology is tied to time-dependent salvage.
The page’s ESC target-time flowchart is represented as decision scenarios.

units.title: 4. Thrombolysis, PCI, Antithrombotics & STEMI Complications
units.guide:
Agent properties, comparative timing and loading doses are kept separate.
Post-lysis physiological changes guide interpretation and anticoagulation.
Mechanical, electrical and NSTE-ACS management follow source order.
